sp_intro_p1: The red panda is the only living member of its own family, Ailuridae, in the order Carnivora. Despite the name, it is not a close relative of the giant panda — its nearest kin are the musteloids (weasels, raccoons, and skunks). In fact, the red panda had the name "panda" first; the giant panda borrowed it later.
sp_intro_p2: Red pandas weigh about 3–6 kg, with a body 50–64 cm long plus a bushy, ringed tail of 28–50 cm. Their most famous feature is the "false thumb" — a sixth "digit" formed from an enlarged wrist bone (the radial sesamoid), used for gripping bamboo. Giant pandas have the same structure, but the two evolved it independently.
sp_intro_p3: They live in temperate forests with bamboo understory from the Himalayas to the mountains of southwestern China, at roughly 2,200–4,800 m elevation, feeding mainly on bamboo leaves and shoots. The IUCN Red List classifies the red panda as Endangered, with fewer than 10,000 mature individuals estimated in the wild and numbers still declining.
sp_two_p1: Traditionally the red panda was treated as a single species with two subspecies: the Himalayan red panda (Ailurus fulgens fulgens) and the Chinese red panda (Ailurus fulgens styani), with the Nujiang (Salween) River long regarded as the boundary between them.
sp_two_p2: In 2020, a whole-genome study by Hu et al. in Science Advances proposed that the two are genetically distinct enough to be separate species — Ailurus fulgens and Ailurus styani — having diverged roughly 200,000-plus years ago, and that the boundary actually lies further west, at the Yarlung Zangbo (Brahmaputra) River rather than the Nujiang.
sp_two_p3: The two-species proposal is still being debated, and the IUCN currently treats red pandas as one species with two subspecies. This is more than a naming dispute: the same researchers who proposed the split argue that if the two are separate species, their extinction risk has to be assessed separately rather than lumped together. This encyclopedia follows the subspecies convention: the "Species" field on each panda's page corresponds to the two forms described here.
sp_fulgens_p1: Found in Nepal, India (around Sikkim and West Bengal), Bhutan, and southern Tibet — the Himalayan range west of the Yarlung Zangbo River.
sp_fulgens_p2: More white on the face (a "whiter-faced" look), a paler forehead, fainter tail rings, a slightly smaller build, and a straighter facial profile.
sp_styani_p1: Found in China's Sichuan and Yunnan provinces, southeastern Tibet, and northern Myanmar — the Hengduan mountain region east of the Yarlung Zangbo River.
sp_styani_p2: A deeper red coat overall, less white on the face with stronger red-and-white contrast, clearly defined tail rings, a larger skull and body, and a more rounded forehead. Zoos in Japan and China hold almost exclusively this subspecies — about 90% of Japanese-born animals in the international studbook are Chinese red pandas — and because this encyclopedia covers Japan most thoroughly, the vast majority of individuals here are Chinese red pandas too.
sp_cmp_range_s: Sichuan, Yunnan, SE Tibet, northern Myanmar
sp_cmp_coat_f: Paler; ochre-tipped hairs on lower back
sp_cmp_note: These are population-level tendencies, not hard rules — individual variation is large, and photos alone are often inconclusive. For zoo animals, go by the studbook records.
sp_breed_p1: Red pandas are seasonal breeders: in the Northern Hemisphere they mate around January–March, and cubs arrive mostly in May–July. Recorded gestation ranges from about 93 to 156 days — a spread that wide because of delayed implantation: the fertilized egg can pause its development and implant later, so that cubs are born in summer when food is most plentiful.
sp_breed_p2: A litter is usually 1–4 cubs, with twins the most common. The twin markers on the {tree} are this phenomenon showing up in our own data.
sp_breed_p3: Newborns arrive fully furred but weigh only about 90–110 g. Their eyes open at around three weeks, they start peeking out of the nest box at around three months, then stay with their mother until nearly a year old, reaching maturity at about 18 months.
sp_breed_p4: Red pandas live about 8–10 years in the wild. In zoos, animals that get through the fragile first year commonly reach 8–12 years, and 15 counts as long-lived: in the international studbook’s 1977–2008 records about a quarter of all animals born reached 12, a little over one in ten reached 15, and only a handful passed 20 — see the "{longevity}" section of our stats page for this encyclopedia’s record holders.
sp_breed_p5: This is also why the "{newborns}" section on our home page only appears from June to November, and why "{stats}" on the stats page peaks in June–July — nearly all Northern Hemisphere red panda cubs arrive in the same season.
sp_consv_p1: The IUCN Red List classifies the red panda as Endangered: fewer than 10,000 mature individuals are estimated in the wild — possibly only a few thousand — with an estimated 40–50% decline over recent decades and numbers still falling. International trade is restricted under CITES Appendix I, which bans commercial international trade.
sp_consv_p1c: Honestly, though, nobody really knows how many are left. Red pandas move at dawn and dusk through remote mountain forest, and no survey has ever covered their whole range — the IUCN says fewer than 10,000, TRAFFIC puts it above 14,000. Even the IUCN assessment itself stops at 2015 and is still flagged on their site as needing an update.
sp_consv_p1d: The laws are there. All five range countries write the red panda into national legislation — Nepal, India and Bhutan on their highest protected list, Myanmar as completely protected, China as a second-class protected species — and internationally it moved up from CITES Appendix II to the commercial-trade ban of Appendix I back in 1995. The hard part was never passing the law; it is making it mean something in forests almost nobody walks through.
sp_consv_p2: The main threats are habitat loss and fragmentation (logging, farmland and roads carving bamboo forest into isolated islands), poaching for pelts, and accidental capture in snares set for other animals; canine distemper spread by free-roaming dogs is also deadly in some areas.
sp_consv_p2b: How badly the habitat has been carved up shows most clearly in protected-area coverage. One study modelling potential range from climate variables put the global figure at roughly 135,000 km² (about 60% in China, 15% in Nepal, around 10% each in Myanmar and Bhutan, and 5% in India), of which only about 28% falls inside existing protected areas — the authors concluded the current network is insufficient. Fieldwork in the eastern Himalayas is more specific: of roughly 12,000 km² mapped as core habitat, just 443 km² lies within protected areas, and the Sela Pass together with the Siang, Dibang and Lohit rivers splits the population into blocks that are hard to move between.
sp_consv_p2c: Poaching is not only about pelts. TRAFFIC compiled 13 seizure cases in China between 2005 and 2017, ten of them (about 77%) traced back to Sichuan; the ten cases from 2005 to 2016 alone involved 35 live and seven dead animals, with live animals bought for an average of about CNY 4,000 — in other words, alongside the fur trade there is a live pet trade. One caveat: seizures only record what was intercepted, and cannot be read directly as the true scale of poaching.
sp_consv_p3: Conservation work includes protecting habitat and reserves, community-based programs (such as Nepal's Forest Guardians), and ex-situ breeding in zoos — zoos worldwide pair animals according to studbooks to maintain a healthy backup population. The residence histories and family trees you see in this encyclopedia are a snapshot of that international effort.
sp_consv_p3b: Nepal's Forest Guardian scheme is the most concrete example of community-based conservation. The Red Panda Network currently has 156 guardians, 20 of them women, looking after 78 community forests; each quarter they patrol with GPS units and camera traps, record red pandas and the species that share their forest, dismantle snares, plant trees and run outreach in their villages. The Puwamajhuwa Community Red Panda Conservation Area, 116 hectares declared in August 2024, is Nepal's first red panda reserve managed by the community itself.
sp_consv_p4: Europe is a good example. When the international studbook was set up in 1979, the captive population was small, unstable and breeding poorly. After the EEP (European Endangered Species Programme) began in 1985, improved husbandry let the population grow steadily; by the end of 2019 it numbered 407 animals across 182 institutions and had come to actively support conservation in the wild.
sp_faq_q1: Can I keep a red panda as a pet?
sp_faq_a1: No. Red pandas are protected under CITES Appendix I and by law in every range country, and commercial trade is banned. They also need large amounts of fresh bamboo, suffer in heat, and are active at dawn and dusk — no home can meet those needs. To see one up close, visit a zoo that keeps them legally.
sp_faq_q2: Are red pandas related to raccoons?
sp_faq_a2: Distantly. Red pandas were once placed in the raccoon family, but now have a family of their own, Ailuridae. Both belong to the superfamily Musteloidea, so raccoons, weasels and skunks are all distant cousins.
sp_faq_q3: Is the Firefox browser named after the red panda?
sp_faq_a3: Yes — "firefox" is one of the red panda's English nicknames, and Mozilla has confirmed that Firefox refers to the red panda. The logo just looks so much like a fox that people are often misled.
sp_faq_a4: No. They are active year-round, getting through winter with a dense coat (even the soles of their feet are furred) and a big tail they wrap around themselves like a blanket. In cold spells they move less, slow their metabolism and sunbathe more — but that isn't hibernation.
sp_health_p1: Every spring, red pandas swap their heavy winter coat for a summer one: it starts around April and settles by early June, with fur shedding from the cheeks, forehead and base of the tail first — so they can suddenly look oddly thin and scruffy. Growing a new coat takes real energy, and they rest more during this period. A patchy-looking red panda at the zoo in summer usually isn't sick; it's just changing outfits (as keepers at Kiryugaoka Zoo in Japan describe).
sp_health_p2: The causes of death in captive red pandas are well documented. The first month is the biggest hurdle: in a 20-year North American necropsy series, newborns under 30 days accounted for 40% of all deaths, and in a Chengdu study nearly 70% of cub deaths occurred within 15 days of birth — mostly respiratory and gut infections triggered by hot, humid summers. That's one reason zoos usually wait until cubs are past their most fragile weeks before introducing them to the public.
sp_health_p2b: The first year is the biggest hurdle. By our own count from the international studbook's 1977–2008 records, global average first-year mortality is around 35%, though the figure has fallen decade by decade — close to 40% in the 1980s, just over 30% in the 2000s. Whether a cub makes it through depends a great deal on each zoo's rearing experience and husbandry.
sp_health_p3: For animals that make it to adulthood, cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death in adult and geriatric red pandas, followed by kidney and gastrointestinal disease. The "heart disease" and "kidney failure" that appear so often in zoo obituaries match these statistics exactly. Acute gastrointestinal emergencies also occur: gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV) has been reported in the veterinary literature, and intussusception appears in zoo obituaries — in 2025, Mel at Tennoji Zoo was still eating normally the night before, then died the next morning of circulatory failure caused by intussusception.
sp_health_p4: Canine distemper is almost always fatal to red pandas — there is even a 1976 case in which a modified-live vaccine itself caused fatal disease. Zoos therefore use only killed or recombinant vaccines and keep stray dogs strictly away, which ties back to the distemper threat mentioned in the conservation section above.
sp_faq_q5: Why does the red panda look patchy and skinny in summer — is it sick?
sp_faq_a5: Usually not — that's leftover spring molt. The winter coat sheds from the cheeks, forehead and tail base first, so molting pandas look thin and scruffy until the summer coat grows in. See "Molting & health" above.
sp_faq_q6: What do red pandas like to eat? Is it true they can taste sweetness?
sp_faq_a6: Bamboo leaves and shoots make up most of the diet; wild red pandas also take fruit, eggs and small animals, and the classic zoo treats are apple slices and bamboo dumplings. The sweet tooth is real: genetic and behavioral studies show red pandas carry a fully functional sweet-receptor gene (Tas1r2), and in taste tests they preferred not only natural sugars but also several artificial sweeteners such as aspartame — the only carnivoran tested to do so, converging with Old World primates. Zoos keep the sweets strictly rationed, though.
sp_faq_q7: Why is the red panda's tail so long and fluffy?
sp_faq_a7: It's a balance pole and a blanket in one. The long tail works as a counterweight when walking along thin branches in the canopy; on cold days a red panda coils it around itself and tucks its nose in to sleep — a duvet it carries everywhere.
sp_faq_q8: Do red pandas make sounds? What do they sound like?
sp_faq_a8: They do — they're just usually quiet, so you need to be close. Red pandas squeal, twitter like birds, and make a signature "huff-quack" — an odd noise halfway between a huff and a duck's quack; when threatened they hiss and grunt. Next time you hear strange quacking from a tree at the zoo, look up.
sp_faq_q9: They're carnivorans — is living on bamboo really okay?
sp_faq_a9: Frankly, it's hard work. Their gut is still a carnivore's short digestive tract, with none of the fermentation equipment herbivores use, so they digest only about a quarter of the bamboo they eat — and it passes through in a matter of hours. The strategy is to eat hard and save hard: 20–30% of their body weight in bamboo leaves and shoots every day, with most of the remaining time spent asleep to conserve energy. That red panda who always seems to be napping at the zoo is, in fact, working hard at life.
sp_faq_q10: Isn't that bright red coat conspicuous in the wild?
sp_faq_a10: It's actually camouflage. In their mountain forests the tree trunks are covered in reddish-brown moss and lichen, so a red panda lying on a branch blends right in; the black belly hides it from predators looking up from below. Field researchers often say that spotting a red panda in its native habitat is remarkably difficult.
sp_faq_a11: Closer to crepuscular — most active around dawn and dusk, and usually asleep in a tree through the day. So a dozing red panda at midday isn't feeling unwell; if you want to see them in action, try soon after opening, late afternoon, or feeding time.
sp_faq_q12: Is there an International Red Panda Day?
sp_faq_a12: There is — the third Saturday of September, launched by the Red Panda Network. Zoos around the world hold outreach events and fundraisers for wild red panda conservation that day. It's also about when cubs born in early summer in the Northern Hemisphere start peeking out of their nest boxes — a perfect excuse for a zoo visit.
about_p1: This site is a non-profit fan project, built by people who simply love red pandas — the fact-checking and corrections, the photo submissions and the reference gathering all come from the day-to-day contributions of fans around the world, together with the maintainer.
about_p2: We want more people to know the red panda — an {species}endangered species{/species} quietly disappearing — and to know {pandas}each individual by name and story{/pandas}. If you enjoy this site, please turn that affection into attention for real red pandas: {zoos}visit them at a zoo{/zoos} and support the people on the front lines of conservation, so that red pandas, in the mountains or in a zoo, can live lives closer to their true nature.
home_about_text: This site is a non-profit fan project built by people who love red pandas. If you enjoy it, please turn that affection into attention for real red pandas.
mv_intro: Red pandas move between zoos throughout their lives — for breeding pairings, habitat renovations and population management. The figures below are derived from each profile’s residence history, covering moves within Japan.
mv_season_note: Transfers peak in {peak} ({n} moves) and all but stop in midsummer, while every birth falls in early summer — the two curves neatly avoid each other.
mv_season_link: See “Breeding and cubs” in the species guide
mv_routes_note: {n} pairs of zoos have exchanged at least one red panda, across {z} zoos.
mv_flow_note: Zoos that breed successfully naturally send out more animals; an uneven balance is expected and says nothing about quality of care.
mv_sec_match: Did the move lead to cubs?
mv_match_headline: {p} of transfers ({n} of {t}) were followed by a cub at the new zoo within three years.
mv_match_note: Counted when a recorded cub of that individual was born at the destination zoo within three years of arrival; only zoos with at least 6 arrivals are listed. Not every transfer is made for breeding.
mv_age_note: Median {n} years ({t} individuals). Red pandas reach sexual maturity at around 18 months, and most set off after that.
mv_note: Only moves within Japan are counted: both the origin and destination must map to a zoo in the registry, and each move is derived from two consecutive entries in a residence history. Month, age and success-rate figures use only moves with a full (year-month-day) date. Individuals flagged as unverified are excluded. Distances are straight-line.
mv_season_scale: Each series is scaled to its own busiest month (transfers peak {a}, births peak {b}) — the comparison is about seasonal shape, not volume.
jp_intro: More than half of the red pandas on this site live in Japan, and its zoos exchange animals more often than anywhere else. These two views cover Japan specifically — the whole family network, and movement between zoos.
jp_stat_note: “Recorded” counts anyone who has lived at a Japanese zoo at some point; “living there now” counts those currently at one ({n} zoos have a resident red panda).
jp_card_tree: Red pandas in Japan form one large interconnected family network. This draws the biggest component — {n} individuals — laid out by generation, pan and zoom to explore.
jp_card_moves: {n} moves between {p} pairs of Japanese zoos, derived from residence histories: when transfers happen, the busiest routes, and whether cubs followed.
jp_trend_intro: Coverage is densest for Japan, so the whole managed population can be traced year by year. Cubs that die soon after birth, before they are ever named, mostly have no entry here, so both the births and the deaths shown here come out low — what follows is the trajectory of the animals on record, not a complete population census.
jp_trend_note: The population peaked at {pn} in {py} and has since fallen to {ln}. Over the same stretch the median age rose from {m0} in {y0} to {m1}, and the share aged 12 or older went from {o0}% to {o1}%.
jp_trend_partial: {y} is not over yet — that column counts only up to today.
jp_trend_caveat: Deaths are structurally undercounted: cub mortality is rarely announced, and only a handful of the Japanese individuals recorded here died before their first birthday. Read “deaths” as animals that reached adulthood — these figures cannot be used to estimate cub survival or average lifespan. For scale: in the international studbook roughly a quarter of the animals born in Japan over the same period did not reach their first birthday, against under 2% among the individuals catalogued here. In the literature this missing slice is far from small; {health} collects what is known about causes of death in captivity.
jp_why_12: Why the line sits at {age}: it is roughly where the breeding years end. Among the Japanese births recorded here the median age of the mother was {mm}, and only {m}% of cubs were born to a mother aged {age} or older ({f}% for fathers). So the animals aged {age} and over are the part of the population unlikely to have more cubs — though usually with several years still ahead of it. (For the breeding cycle itself, see {breeding}.)
jp_trend_shape: The total alone hides something, though. Since the {py} peak the population is down by only {d} — but that is two opposite movements cancelling out: {dy} fewer animals under {age}, and {do} more aged {age} or older. What is disappearing is almost entirely the young, and those who remain are growing old together.
sp_consv_p5: A backup population does not sustain itself. Japan, the country covered most thoroughly here, shows the other side of that: transfers between zoos and planned pairings hold the network together, yet births have fallen in recent years and the population is shrinking and ageing fast — see {japan} for the year-by-year picture.
jp_sub_intro: Of the {n} red pandas currently in Japan, {s} are {sn} and {f} are {fn}. Most red pandas in zoos anywhere belong to the former, and in Japan the imbalance is especially stark.
jp_sub_one: All {f} of those {fn} live at {zoo} — currently the only place in Japan where the nominate subspecies can be seen.
sp_fulgens_p3: In Europe, North America and Australasia this is the subspecies you are most likely to meet: in the international studbook (data through 2008) virtually every captive-born animal in Europe is a Himalayan red panda, and it predominates in North America and the Southern Hemisphere too. Japan is the exception — the country covered most thoroughly here currently holds only a handful, all of them at a single zoo; see {japanSub} for the current picture.
sp_breed_p1b: The calendar flips with the hemisphere: in Southern Hemisphere zoos cubs are born mainly in December and January. In the international studbook’s 1977–2008 records, 98% of animals born in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa arrived between December and February, and not one in May–July — the same species, shifted half a year by the hemisphere.
stats_dam_age_note: {n} births from {d} dams; youngest {min}, median {med}, oldest {max} years. Counted only where both the dam’s and the cub’s birth dates are known.
stats_death_age_note: {n} individuals with a known date of death; the median age at death is {med} years — {p3}% died at 15–19, {p2}% at 10–14 and {p4}% at 20 or over. Cubs that die before their first birthday are mostly never catalogued here, so this shows how long red pandas live once they have grown up; it is not a survival rate.
